en: On the glorious Sandalwood Mountain, which is beautiful to the entire earth,
there is a delightful abode of the Gandharvas called Kanakanagarī;
it is adorned with golden pleasure-pavilions whose peaks scrape the very sky.
In that city of the gods, which bears the count of hundreds of branch-cities,
there was a Gandharva maiden named Kuvalayavatī; I consider her to be a victorious weapon of Smara, softer even than a flower.
Upon seeing King Lakṣmaṇa, the conqueror of the world,
the young girl immediately became subject to the flower-bowed god;
even among her childhood companions, she did not reveal her passion for the Mind-born.

Pale and emaciated, the timid woman passed some days; then, as spring had begun in a manner quite contrary to her wishes, she, filled with intense longing, made a request to the Malaya breeze with a bow, so that it might depart for another land.
From you come the life-breaths of all the worlds; by nature you are swift, O Wind, and they declare you to be immediately after the mind.
Therefore, indeed, this state of being a petitioner has been directed toward you by me.
Generally, alms-seeking becomes fruitless indeed with those such as you.
Having observed the state of Rāmacandra, distressed by separation, Añjaneya went to the further shore of even the lord of rivers for his sake, O Wind-god.
Therefore, as your father proceeds with unimpeded course for my sake,
how many yojanas indeed lie between the land of Gauḍa and Mount Malaya?
There, during the season of flowers, he must certainly be attended by you.
The Gauḍa country has its courtyard of the sky covered by dense gardens;
therefore, tell me of your state, O King, for the sake of saving my life—for indeed, the manifestation of those like you in the three worlds is for the benefit of others. (6)
Having stolen the priceless fragrance from these sandalwood trees,
depart quickly from the forests of the Malaya foothills before these serpents, who are devoted to the arts of amorous play, arrive.
Under the pretext of enjoyment, the envious drink you up drop by drop.
Having passed the vicinity of the Sandalwood Mountain for a distance of two gavyūtis,
you must go to the Pāṇḍya country, which is a certain ornament of the world.
There, on the bank of the Tāmraparṇī river, marked by rows of charming areca trees, you should visit the city renowned by the name Uragapura,
where women, at the end of their amorous dalliance, are exhausted with their creeper-like arms relaxed. 8.103–104ab.
Shaking off the weight of their unaccustomed braids with their natural charm,
the Malaya breezes, arriving at once through the lattice-windows of the palace to dispel the sweat of fatigue, become fans for her in this place. 9.
If you should go to the Setu out of curiosity for the pleasure-mountain that serves as a long chain for the elephants of the ocean— the wives of the city of the serpents—
it shines with affection as the cause of consolation for the life of the daughter of the Earth.

There you will see the lofty and stainless lineage of Rāmeśvara, which is like a single arm of the earth extended toward Laṅkādvīpa, and from which the moon— the crest-jewel of the wrathful Gaurī— was drawn by her sprout-like hand.
Where the unevenness of the three folds at the waist of the courtesans betokens the trembling of the hands of the Creator as he fashioned the position of their girdles;
Then go to Kāñcīpura, the ornament of the southern quarter, where at night the five-arrowed god (Kāma), holding his bow in his hand, becomes like a sentry keeping the citizens awake. 12.

When her fine Chinese upper garment has slipped away due to the impetuosity of her eagerness for water-sports, she immediately offers the edge of her cloth under the guise of a mass of foam, as if it were a playful smile turned dark by the clouds.

O Wind, I believe that for the women of the Cola country, whose breasts are so firm, liberation from the exhaustion of intense lovemaking— attained by you as if by a friend with waves for hands— will soon become difficult to obtain.
Or who does not stumble upon their cheeks—the regions of their temples adorned with dark indigo clinging to the arrangement of their curls and made slippery by the liquid of sandalwood paste? 14.
Having abandoned the river-bank bower beloved by the immodest women, having left the girdle behind...
Follow that Kāverī river, whose banks are made resonant by rows of birds;
its water is more pleasant to the touch than the embrace of a beloved, clearer even than the moonlight, and lighter even for one whose mind is intent on begging. 15.
She who is as naturally beautiful as the Ganges, attaining a pallor from the sandalwood paste on the breasts of Kerala women during their playful baths—
she is like the river that constantly trembles with fear born from the ocean's frequent lapses in its course.

If the young women of the South perform water-sports in her waist-deep current— she who knows the flavor of their words of love as they fall at her feet with trembling brows— then she is like a river of grace.
With drops of water white as jasmine, create for them a lattice of pearls upon their breasts where the necklaces have slipped away due to the tossing of the waves;
and [create] Mount Mālyavān with its smooth, dark, and heavy rocks.
One might see before one’s eyes the mass of hair of the Earth, as if it were bristling;
even today, the mountain ridges there, shattered by the waters of the counter-cataracts, indicate the falling tears of Sītā’s husband, whose grief was immense. 18.
O Māṇḍakarṇa, you should go to that lake of Indra called Pañcāpsaras, whose shores are beautiful with *sarala* trees and which has stolen away the intense heat [of summer]; there,
even today, the series of charming songs of the celestial maidens resounds.
With their outskirts delightful with groves abounding in *krīḍāśoka*, *kramuka*, and *bahula* trees, they will cause longing for the herds of deer that have come there out of former affection;
these lands will bring you joy at every step as you set forth on your journey.

Leaving behind the Andhra country, where the Godāvarī river is closely embraced by the wives of the countryside, the forest groves— filled with ponds and causing travelers to wander incessantly out of their longing for the love of low-born women bowing under the weight of their full, high breasts— [now appear]. 20.
Follow the Kalinga king to that capital city named Nagari;
there, at the conclusion of their dalliance, dispel the physical exhaustion of the courtesans whose eyes are half-closed as you alight upon their pleasure-windows. 21.
You should go to the shore of the ocean, which possesses rows of many steps formed by the accumulation of dancing waves, and where the lines of *pūga* trees bend under the weight of their fruit;
there, you will hear the music, pleasing to the ear, of the singing celestial women (*siddhāṅganā*).
From place to place, gently produce those sounds that are not followed by echoes;
enjoy the foothills of the Vindhya, where the luster of the creepers and young shoots withers from the breezes of the sighs of the young celestial nymphs sporting in the bowers.
Beholding the faces of the wives of hunters, who are not overly clever,
their eyes darting with fear at the trumpeting of intoxicated scent-elephants;
roam as you please in this place delightful by its own nature, where the lofty trees are crowded with birds.
In that forest, which is fond of the embrace of Mount Vindhya, even the proud Bhilla women—
who, having heard the cruel cry of elephants in secret,
have cast their vine-like arms around the necks of their husbands— become possessed of human pride.

Go to the Revā, whose banks and groves have been sprinkled by Śabarī women who delight in their own spontaneous play, and which possesses a bamboo forest as dark as a young parrot; for they consider it, in its surrounding regions, a place where the mature women of the countryside [find pleasure].
Even the playful pride of love is an obstacle for young men. If you wish to bring the amorous glances of Kerala women before your eyes,
go to that city famous in the world by the name of Yayāti.
Where the *nāgavallīs* (betel vines), their stems firmly embraced by *kramuka* trees, teach young maidens the art of the embrace of a beloved;
[a city] whose outskirts are washed by the surges of the Gaṅgā and which is adorned with rows of palaces.
The Suhma country will experience intense wonder at you;
there, the palm-leaf, as delicate as a digit of the new moon, shall become an ear-ornament for the wives of the brahmins, providing a delight to their ears. (27)
In that Suhma country dwells the Lord Murāri, the source of the sport of Lakṣmī, who was consecrated by the King of the Devas as the sovereign of the gods;
near whom the women of the city repeatedly carry play-lotuses in their hands.
The courtesans, naturally beautiful, will cause you to suspect them to be Lakṣmī herself.
After you have passed beyond the white mansions belonging to the attendants of the Lord of Wealth,
you shall behold that faultless city of the one whose crest is the crescent moon.
Where the courtesans bear upon their laps the mark of the digit of the moon— the ornament of their husbands— under the guise of many beloved nail-scratches;
there, on the banks of the celestial river, [they worship] the priceless preceptor of the Raghu dynasty.
Having bowed to the God, whose limbs are as delightful as those shared with the Daughter of the Mountain, depart—
He, upon entering the range of vision of women with beautiful creeper-like brows, causes the pride born of love for their lovers to melt away.
Between that sacred field and the river of heaven,
the Setubandha— the kinsman of the glory of the illustrious King Ballāla—
is to be resorted to by people who have ascended [the mountain] for the purpose of bathing in the celestial river.
There, the city of the immortals shines as if drawn near in two ways;
then you should resort to that Gaṅgā, who carries in her wave-hands a mirror of clusters of foam, and who is adorned by mature swans upon her banks.

As her beloved returns to the ocean, she who is restless with love appears somewhat haughtily, as if intending to seize him by the hair; such is the state of the young women who have fallen passionately into the water-sports. 32.
Of the beautiful women falling into the delightful aquatic play...

Then, bowing with devotion, go to that region which purifies the world, where the goddess Tapanatanayā (the Daughter of the Sun) flows forth from the Bhāgīrathī, her dark hue intensified again by the musk on [Gaṅgā’s] breasts being washed away by the waves. 33.
Beholding that river of the gods as it glided forth from the womb of the waters— naturally crooked, displaying its whirling eddies—
the earth should not become despondent with the fear that she has been released by a female serpent with white hoods.
Everyone is afraid of a serpent; how much more so one such as you?
While the playful women sport impetuously in the water there, create the slipping away of their garments from their breasts with the hands of the waves.
And may the playful, soft smiles of those women, agitated by the sight of their lover, immediately become the ends of their upper garments.
[May] the military camp, the lofty capital named Vijayapura, [prosper].

Upon seeing that king, the conqueror of the world, you shall attain such a state as when the breeze from the Ganges immediately provides a massage to the limbs of the city women at the conclusion of their amorous dalliance. (36)

Upon the smooth, naturally beautiful *vaḍabhī-śālabhañjī* statues above the assembly hall, the fair-browed women, hidden by their eagerness for play, are somehow discovered by their lovers; as the tips of the lotus-hands of their beloveds touch them in secret, they break out into buds of horripilation. 37.
In that place, betel-nut trees were planted in the courtyards by the city women, who had constructed elevated basins with smooth, dark, and delightful gems;
their roots were watered at night by waters that arrived without effort.

They did not even look at the water offered from the hands of their female attendants. Under that king’s protection, the citizens became free from fear in both worlds, for they were naturally pure through contact with the Ganges.
Then, from those young women whose sprouts of anger had taken root through lovers' quarrels,
and whose faces were both beautiful and fearsome due to the knitting of their brows, they departed;
having taken from their ears that [garland] which had been set in place, now marked by teardrops mixed with collyrium.

There, a palm-leaf marked with vermilion from the jeweled earrings resting upon the lower lips of women— bound by a bond of lotus-fiber cords withered by the heat of separation— becomes a love-letter to their beloved. 40.
There, out of affection for their husbands, charming wives— disregarding the exhaustion of the Jina— would, with the intent of wiping away the drops of sweat produced by spontaneous lovemaking,
place the moon-like lusters of their breasts into the lap of the wine that had entered the lattice-work of the windows.
The clusters of beautiful women, who delight in the passion for the sport of swings, are drawn away by the illusion that the saffron unguents on their breasts— whose heat has increased—
are the heavy loads of lovely yak-tail fans.

Where, for young lovers wandering in the thick darkness while longing for their beloveds, the pleasure-pools with their shallow waters, the nights adorned with garlands of *mālatī* flowers, and the dense moonlight bring incessant joy. (42)

There, at the end of night, the lac-dye trickling from the feet of the city women on the public roads could not be distinguished from the rays of the young sun, lovely as clusters of red *aśoka* blossoms. 43
With jewels such as pearls, emeralds, sapphires, and saugandhika stones, with conch shells suitable for fashioning bracelets for young girls,
and with corals— the ocean whose waters were drunk up without remainder by the sage who is the beloved of Lopāmudrā.
In that city, which is a mine of jewels, Fortune takes away all calamities;
there, young women wear emerald necklaces that have become mute as they rest upon breasts smeared with musk-paste.
Having lit the fire of the god of love with the wick of her heart by means of floods of oil,

women go to the houses of their beloveds even in thick darkness. That which was laboriously made into a leaf for the writing of the script of immodesty by the large-eyed woman— [the rest of the verse follows].

Where, as soon as their beloveds bow at their feet, the streams of tears from the eyes of proud women— dark with mingled collyrium— are released, as if they have suddenly washed away their hearts. 46.

At their very head, having lost his pride, he was unable even to stand before them; what then can be said of the splendor and prowess of the Flower-Arrowed God, with those amorous gestures charming through the casting of glances so skillful in the play of beautiful brows?
Even that place where you have gone has become a state of servitude for the beautiful-eyed women;
for while you, the preceptor of the mind-born god, remain there, those fawn-eyed maidens are seen enjoying the playful delights of the swings in their well-arranged gardens.

At the close of day, the interiors of the palaces, filled with the smoke of burning agallochum, seemed like the armies of Kandarpa, eager to conquer the celestial nymphs, practicing a flight through the forest of the sky with great impetuosity.
48. At the close of day, the interiors of the palaces, filled with the smoke of burning agallochum... [The provided text fragment ends here].
There, the smoke exhaled from the lattices, dark as a water-laden cloud,

creates the suspicion that it is a spreading mass of darkness— caused by contact with the moonlight from the faces of the city women who have suddenly mounted their balconies in the fervor of their playful curiosity—
at midnight, when the charming words of their dear companions have become futile. (49) At night, when the lovely speech of their beloved friends has proved in vain...

There, the moon, repeatedly approaching and using its rays as a hand, settles the lovers' quarrels of the youths dwelling on the tops of pleasure-palaces— quarrels in which the garlands have fallen away from the *kuvalaya* lotuses used as ear-ornaments due to their anger. 50.

There, during the exchange of amorous play according to their own desire, the women perceive the naturally beautiful inner petal of the *ketakī* flower— which has slipped from their ears— due to the friction caused by their earrings swinging back and forth in the movement of their union.
The wise perceive her speech as a single fragment of the moon of her face broken off and placed directly before them;
her side-glances are nectar for the ears accompanied by the play of her eyebrows; her form is worthy of being held in the uplifted palms, and her gestures are tender and charming.
You should go to the delightful palace of the Indra of the earth’s circle,
upon the peaks of whose mansions— which are friends to the mountains— the streaks of lightning, when the clouds rest there, repeatedly display the splendor of the Vaijayantī banner. 53.

Upon its banks, as the young women sporting there— whose dark curls were like smooth, split sapphires— displayed a line of hair as lovely as that of the Earth-goddess, which seemed fashioned from those very stones and spread across it.
I believe that even the royal swans become heavy in their playful movements.
You should serve the King— who is like the god of love himself, visibly consecrated with the rite of sovereignty— with fly-whisks during times of distress.

He, by the expansive movement of his glistening, flashing sword-blade, shared a friendship with the eyes of the wives of his enemy clans; he, out of eagerness for those who were maddened by the sight of the peerless battle— (55) —[attained] the eyes... [of the wives].

I imagine that for the celestial women, whose garment-hems have fallen unnoticed, the spreading clouds of dust kicked up by the hooves of the swift horses of the rain-showers immediately cling to their jar-like breasts, serving as a covering between them. 56.
With their necks bent and their lotus-faces pressed against the vine-like lotus-stalks of their arms,
these women drank him in from all sides with side-glances as long as a row of blue-lotus petals— drinking him out of both fear and curiosity that he was the king of the Sena dynasty.
During the sudden flight of the city at the onset of the enemies, she was filled with the cries of the city women;
and in her pleasure-house, she bore the likeness of her beloved, long painted there, as if it were a mental image accompanied by the shrieks of birds.
The mature women of the enemy’s city bear their long, drooping tresses under the guise of the tufts of dūrvā grass grown upon the palaces;
even as they offer resistance through a rising crop of horripilation when struck by the feet of their husbands in playful anger, they nonetheless cause them distress.
Why do you wander thus upon the mountain forest floor, where the sprouts of darbha grass are so cruel, for such is the lamentation of the female parrots in the city of your enemy?
If, at that time, he should spend even a third part of the day anywhere—

The king, contemplating obstacles, is capable of keeping [the matter] secret; therefore, O Wind, you must not reveal my message to him at that time. When the mind is consumed by urgent business, there is no room for dalliance.
Therefore, O gentle one, having found some opportune moment, you should approach the King in private and speak softly with humility;
for even in other matters, a portion of the task is made manifest by those who act out of affection.
If he is capable of attaining success even at such an occasion, how much more so among kings?
On a peak of the Śrīkhaṇḍa mountain dwells a certain Gandharva realm; there resides a single woman, Kuvalayavatī by name, who is the most honored among women.
O King, consider the Malaya valley breeze as her messenger— that single wind which unites pairs of lovers who have been separated from one another.
Having swiftly conquered the southern lords of the earth, O Lord, [you now enjoy this breeze].
When her lover had returned from the slopes of the Malaya mountains and traveled far away, taking her heart with him,
the pressure of her tears suddenly blocked the path of her eyes, as she thought, "The purpose of his coming has been in vain."
Having placed her feet upon the ground and fixed her eyes upward with curiosity,
that slender-limbed woman is seen from the palace pinnacle gazing toward the horizon— naturally beautiful through contact with you— with her neck uplifted, as if beholding something indescribable.

O you who bring delight to the eyes of all women, at the time when you were brought within the range of vision by that bold-eyed doe— your eyes being repeatedly veiled by welling tears as she longed to go near you— [you were seen]. 64.
From that time forward, her heart filled with the distress of feverish longing,
she finds no confidence or solace even in the most beautiful places. (65) By Fate, which made her waist so slender it could be grasped by a single fist—

O King, I believe that slender-bodied woman, now bearing the emaciated state born of intense separation, was fashioned by the Flower-Bowed God as a bowstring for his bow; she has now become like a creeping vine. 66
"Tell me, O tremulous one, what kind of lover dwells within you?"—
when her friends thus repeatedly questioned her with effort regarding her beloved,
she heaved a deep sigh and, somehow restraining the flow of her tears, [remained silent].
With her gaze fixed upon the wall of the house where Love has been painted, she immediately experiences the delusion that it is a love letter sent by you,
even though it is merely a palm-leaf fallen from the ear-ornament of her dear companion.
Moreover, she repeatedly asks even her pet parrot for news of you;
indeed, how can she, whose longing has grown so intense, take account of her noble lineage?
She is so consumed by anger that she will not even allow the blue lotus to serve as an ornament for her eye.
Exhausted by the flower garlands, she does not even cover her creeper-like arm; and, startled by the lotus— which is the very cause of the abundance of heat placed upon her heart—
she suddenly closes her eyes and trembles even at the hand of her friend.
Practicing her art, she lies upon a bed of fresh flowers and grass at its edge;
she causes the carp to leap in agitation from the drying mud-beds,
and she brings tears to her eyes like water-drops falling from the stalks of her lotus-eyes.
I think that girl will somehow pass the days;
having received from you an inner heat that cannot be severed even by icy waters, and which is incurable even by streams of sandalwood powder.
Bewildered by their extreme resemblance to the flower-arrowed god [Kāma], they incur his reproach;
for even those who are well-settled might become distracted, so what need be said of those agitated by separation?
There is hatred toward dwelling in the pleasure-grove, and a prohibition against sandalwood water.

The rejection of the breeze from the fan of fresh lotus leaves has occurred; how it was somehow produced in her through the thought of you as a friend—this alone is the means for the cessation of the force of her fainting during your separation. 72.
She harbors hatred for the moon, shows no regard for her mass of hair,
casts her necklace far away, and takes delight in reviling sandalwood;
O King, she can only with great difficulty speak of her own condition regarding you.
Filled with intense agitation, she passes her days in the contemplation of poetry.
First, he entered the path of her eyes, causing the lashes to stiffen; then, kissing the region of her cheek, he drank from her bimba-fruit lower lip.
Even while embracing her neck and lying upon the bed of her bosom, what indeed does her tears not do during separation from you?
They reduce the limbs of that gazelle-eyed woman to mere ashes.

I know that even though the fire of love was fanned by her sighs during our separation, O King, it was surely due to the power of the waters from the basin of her eyes— waters as cooling as you, who dwell perpetually within her heart. 75
When the night had almost reached its end, the young woman, her eyes slightly closed,
somehow obtained you before her in a dream with intense passion; as she embraced her own body, she suddenly awoke.
She turns her face away from the faces of her friends, trembling with shame;
the young woman avoids the pleasure grove, which is more delightful than the moon, from afar,
and she does not engage in conversation anywhere with her circle of companions.
For the sake of protection from the arrows of Love, that poor girl holds only a play-board against her breast, which is beautiful with the reflection of you;
she casts her eyes upon the moon, while tears fall like a rainy day.

Desiring to smell the fragrance of bakula flowers with her deep sighs, and wishing to hear the humming of bees, she was protected by fainting; seeing such a state, who indeed would not be overcome with compassion for her? (78)
Compassion throbs within her mind during separation; she feels detachment toward passion, constant indignation toward the flower-arrowed god of love, and self-contempt for herself.
Thus, like a wretched painting, she clings to these various states as if they were situated within her own limbs.
It reveals a state of being fixed with exclusive devotion toward you:
(79) previously, even the conversations of her friends were repeatedly delightful with love;
but now that you have become utterly devoid of compassion, there is not even a hope for reunion.
O Lord, for her, the very fainting fit— which causes her to forget the sorrow born of separation—
becomes the sole constant support for her life.
O King, because she cannot reach him with her hands, she has no means of experiencing his touch.

Although washed by the streams of tears from her eyes upon the curve of her cheek, the moon— borne in her heart as she approaches the region of her breasts— assumes the likeness of the royal parasol atop a king’s head. 81.
Now that the winter season has passed with difficulty, for me who cannot even catch a breeze coming from your presence—
when the cuckoos are eager and vocal with their playful warbling— who will protect me?
O fortunate one, tell her this in the month of Caitra: "The means for saving her life is at hand.
The mind of that lotus-eyed woman enters again and again into the cruel fire of love, while the pair of her eyes is submerged in a flood of tears.

O King, lover of the lady that is the circle of the earth, for her who is distressed by intense separation from you, that wretched cheek has become thin and pale, as if smeared with ashes. 83. O King, from your presence—
May the thread of hope remain, for the thread of love is difficult to find;
yet from misery to even greater misery—alas! even sleep, that messenger of dreams, does not approach the boundary of her eyes for even a moment. (84)

The very breaths, which were once uniquely capable of inflaming the fire of Love, have now returned from the vicinity of her breasts— those breasts whose fullness is like sandalwood paste— and they excessively torment her, whose heart is agitated by longing.
In this very same way, infamies are brought forth by the Malaya breezes.
And she, longing for the pleasure of remembering your face and being exceedingly timid, makes the moon— the lord of the twice-born— a fit object of reproach with her showers of moonlight.
Moreover, O Sundara, having thought of you, the two physicians of the gods feel aversion;
for generally, such is the disposition of one whose death is imminent. Out of that distaste, the dark-eyed lady [rejects] the golden palm leaves.
She wears an ear-ornament that is naturally beautiful because it has been rejected;
having suddenly perceived a certain frailty in her limbs, it was as if the God of Love, out of fear, had cast off the string of his bow. 87.
Indeed, because of the offense of sandalwood— which has been her friend since birth— she does not frequent the forests of the Malaya foothills; moreover,
being slender in all her limbs, she dwells above, as if out of hatred for Madana himself.
Possessed by a fit of passion, she allows no room for pleasure in her mind; she casts her gaze toward the pleasure garden while suppressing her tears with effort,
and with her limbs anointed with sandalwood paste, she immerses herself in the thick moonlight.
This wind rushes toward the pleasure-pool in agitation; or rather, what desperate act will women not perform when separated from their lovers?

The vital breaths do not abandon her at all, even though she is emaciated by longing; or rather, having found such an embrace around the neck of women, who in this world would be able to leave her, even if their hearts were alienated? (90)
The heat of her body has faded, the stream of tears from her eyes has ceased, and the restless movements of her limbs have come to rest;
thus, as the feverish passion born of separation has been stilled in that fawn-eyed woman.
Her sighs were further increased, becoming an obstacle to her peace.
Oppressed in the pleasure garden by the female cuckoos singing their fifth note,
her form grew faint under the Malaya breeze at the windows of the pleasure chambers.
That timid-eyed woman does not set foot anywhere even for a single moment;
truly, even the three worlds do not bring joy to those who are suffering.
Though she possesses knowledge that allows her movement to be unimpeded everywhere, she [does not come] to you.
O fortunate one, fearing a refusal, she does not approach you suddenly;
for kings, even when their minds are naturally passionate, do not shine when they are terrified by a wife in whom deep love has taken root, as if she were another woman. 93
The sandalwood paste applied to the slope of her breasts immediately dries up as her slender body is consumed by the fierce fire of love;
what is the use of many words for one whose inner state has been elevated to such an extreme?
"The means of protecting the life of the lotus-eyed one depends upon you. When this is said, the God of Love, his body thrilled with joy, rises up and embraces you firmly and affectionately.
By these words, tender with compassion, even stones attain softness; how much more so one who is naturally gentle?
O Wind, having immediately placed your joined palms upon your head as a mark of humility, [speak] a little... 95.
That King of Gauḍa should be addressed by you in private on my behalf:
he will listen with an attentive mind, for the words of devoted women produce waves of nectar for one who is beloved. (96)
O Lord, displaying Your manifest form at my side, behind me, and even before me, You are the sovereign of the worlds, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow;
why then do You not show favor to me, whose mind is inclined toward devotion?
No one other than the slayer of Kaiṭabha is capable of creating such an array of forms.
Having approached me while my eyes were closed on the terrace of the palace in front of my friends, you placed me beyond the reach of words.
Therefore, O fortunate one, you should act in such a way that we do not become objects of reproach among the virtuous;
for truly, wise men in this world do not abandon a maiden after having defiled her. (98) When the rite of Gaurī’s marriage had been performed, [he who] possessed abundant joy...

O King, may there be for you from afar a bond of love, skillful in solicitation, like that of the flower-bannered god [Kāma] newly created by the conqueror of Tripura; and by what merit might I be permitted even to massage your feet? 99.
Has this message been kept in your mind, O long-lived one? Or what more need be said, my dear friend, regarding the various forms of begging you have devised for me?
For those like you, whose minds are solely intent on the welfare of others, [even] tears mixed with...
Those who have incurred [his] displeasure certainly do not often escape his plaintive reproaches. 100.
He who was the emperor of the kings of poets received from the Lord of Gauḍa a phalanx of elephants, a golden creeper, and a yak-tail whisk with a golden handle.

For the sake of pleasing all connoisseurs, the wise Śrī Dhoyīka uttered this poetic composition, which was like a great mantra of Sarasvatī: "The assembly of all poets shall be held in speech according to the Vaidarbha style. 101. In the assembly, the Vaidarbha manner is to be used by all poets.
May my wealth be such that it is enjoyed with affection on the banks of the Gaṅgā;
may I have love for the virtuous and the mastership of poetry in the assembly of kings;
and may there be devotion to the feet of the Lord of Lakṣmī even in another birth. 102
As long as Śambhu bears a body shared with Girijā;
as long as the flower-arrowed god wields his victorious bow made of blossoms;
and as long as the Kadamba tree remains the witness to the amorous sports of the youthful consort of Rādhā.
May this play of words by the poet Narapati endure as long as life lasts!
Fame has been won in the assembly of the learned, cool kings have been [described], and several compositions of speech that distill nectar have been created. 103.
Now, on the bank of the river of the immortals, somewhere at the foot of a mountain,
I desire to spend my days with a mind intent on the practice of Brahman.
(104) The poem entitled *Pavanadūta*, composed by the illustrious King of Poets, Dhoyī, is completed.
